newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Internet not viable option for trading - HK bourse.
newsitem.headline: Internet not viable option for trading - HK bourse.

text.p: The Internet lacks the controls and guarantees which would allow it to challenge traditional stock markets as forums for professional traders, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange said on Tuesday.

"I believe trading via the Internet, even at its best, is suitable only for retail purposes -- unlike the market provided by the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, which has a proven track record and an established regulatory framework to ensure fairness and integrity for all market participants," chief executive Alec Tsui told an Asian cybertrading conference.
The two-day conference, which began on Tuesday in Hong Kong, was organised to address issues such as raising capital and trading stock on the Internet.
"I don't in my life time see (the Internet) as becoming a world class financial service," said Maurice Newman, chairman of the Australian Stock Exchange Ltd.
He said people turning to the Internet were looking for regulatory arbitrage. "They don't want highly visible markets, they don't want markets which are transparent," he said.

"The Internet itself as an alternative, that is without the participation of those markets which already have a reputation, which are already accepted as being reliable markets for those people who deal in them, I have certainly great reservations," Newman added.
Both Tsui and Newman saw the Internet as a way for exchanges to deliver financial services.
The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong recently issued a consultation paper in which addressed further automation of its trading system and proposed an order routing system.

"Order routing is the Exchange's concept of Cyber Trading," said Tsui. He said it would allow investors to place orders and accept trade confirmations over the telephone, via a terminal, or through the Internet.
But Hong Kong's financial markets watchdog has proposed a series of more ambitious virtual trading options to take advantage of cybertechnology.

It has proposed a new Securities and Futures bill which includes an option which would authorise investors to bypass stockbrokers in certain situations to improve market efficiency, Securities and Futures Commission executive director David White said.

"What we have to recognise here in Hong Kong is that these electronic markets are going to increase in importance and we need to be able to have some control over them," White, who was also speaking at the conference, told Reuters.
